one_liner: Experimental Zig async runtime on libxev; its 1.5x-96x 'faster than Tokio' table is not backed by real Tokio runs.
what_it_does: Zokio is a Tokio-inspired async runtime for Zig 0.14 that sits on top of libxev. You wrap plain functions with async_fn / async_fn_with_params to get pollable futures, spawn them on a runtime, and wait for them with await_fn. It also ships scheduler, memory-pool, net, fs and timer modules. The API is Zig-only and has nothing in common with Tokio's Rust API beyond naming.
how_it_is_fast: The claimed techniques are comptime-generated future state machines (async_fn_with_params turns a function into a struct with a state enum and poll()), a work-stealing scheduler with a LIFO slot and batch stealing, tiered object pools for allocation, and libxev (io_uring/kqueue/IOCP) for I/O. The multi-billion ops/s rows come from awaiting futures that are ready on the first poll (e.g. value * 2) in a tight loop. That compiles to an inlined call, so it measures function-call cost rather than runtime work, and the guide even lists 'Future Polling' at infinite ops/s.
when_to_use: Reading or prototyping how comptime can generate future/poll state machines in Zig 0.14.
Studying one way to wrap libxev (kqueue/io_uring/IOCP) behind a Tokio-like spawn/await API.
Hobby code pinned to Zig 0.14 where you are willing to vendor, fix and own the MIT-licensed source.
Mining ideas for a Zig work-stealing scheduler config (LIFO slot, steal batch size, spin-before-park knobs).
when_not_to_use: Any decision that relies on 'faster than Tokio': no valid same-machine comparison exists in the repo.
Production services: it is self-described v0.1.0, lists 'Production readiness' and 'Stable API' as v1.0 goals, has 5 stars, no filed issues, and no commits since 2025-07-22.
Workloads that await futures which really pend on I/O, because await_fn spin-waits the calling thread or times out/panics (see gotchas).
Projects on Zig 0.15 or newer: src/lib.zig uses `usingnamespace`, which Zig 0.15 removed.
Rust code: this is not a Tokio replacement; there are Rust siblings with real Tokio measurements.

integration.form: module (Zig package added via build.zig.zon, built from source)
integration.dependencies: libxev, expected at deps/libxev. At HEAD that path is a git submodule entry with no .gitmodules file, so a fresh clone or the README's archive/main.tar.gz install has no libxev source. A commented-out entry pins libxev commit 3df9337.
integration.min_toolchain: Zig 0.14.0 (minimum_zig_version); effectively 0.14.x only, since the code uses `usingnamespace` (not verified by building)
integration.platforms: README claims Linux (io_uring), macOS/BSD (kqueue) and Windows (IOCP) through libxev; every published number is macOS on Apple Silicon
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the README describes a multi-threaded work-stealing scheduler but gives no thread-safety guarantees for its types

gotchas: await_fn with no event loop polls at most 10 times with spin hints, then returns error.Timeout for error-union outputs, returns silently for void, and calls @panic for anything else. With an event loop it waits by spinning on an atomic flag (the source comments call this a 'simplified implementation') and logs at info level on every call.

`zig build tokio-vs-zokio` only runs Tokio if cargo works. Otherwise it silently substitutes hard-coded 'literature' constants (task_scheduling 800K, memory_allocation 5M, io_operations 400K ops/s) and prints them as Tokio results. Its generated Tokio 'I/O' test is a 1-1000 ns tokio::time::sleep, which Tokio's millisecond timer turns into ~1 ms waits.

Benchmark bodies do not measure what their names say. The 'optimized I/O' benchmark memsets and checksums a 1 KB stack buffer and never uses the I/O driver it initializes. The scheduling benchmark reports the max of the enqueue, execution and wall-clock rates. Its task poll resets a local counter, so any task with more than 10 work units returns .pending on every poll and never completes (49 of 50 tasks).

The docs disagree with each other. The English guide says Apple M1 Pro, while the README and the Chinese docs say M3 Pro. The same numbers carry different row labels (e.g. 3.8B is 'await_fn' in one place and 'nested async' in another). Several Chinese analysis reports in docs/ contradict the headline table (tokio-comparison.md, final-tokio-vs-zokio-analysis.md, memory-allocation-gap-analysis.md).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Essentially never for performance reasons. If you need a Rust runtime that measurably beats Tokio, monoio (~1.86x Tokio echo QPS) or exec-rs (10-26% more req/s) publish real same-setup runs, and ringline gives an honest cell-by-cell comparison against tuned Tokio. Consider Zokio only as a Zig 0.14 learning codebase; for production Zig I/O, using libxev directly avoids Zokio's unfinished await path.
verified_claims_summary: docs/en/performance.md reports Zig 0.14.0 -O ReleaseFast microbenchmarks on an Apple M1 Pro against a 'Tokio Baseline' column, but no Tokio run in the repo produced that column. The 1.5M figure matches the hard-coded future_composition constant (1_500_000) in getLiteratureBaseline and is reused elsewhere as a Tokio memory baseline. The 192K figure matches Zokio's own standard-allocator result (~190K ops/s), which docs/PROJECT_OVERVIEW.md describes as '85x faster than standard', not faster than Tokio. The ~100M/~50M/~25M/~2M/~15K rows have no Tokio benchmark code at all. The only recorded real Tokio runs (docs/tokio-stress-test-analysis.md: 0.41-1.10M task ops/s, 1.39-1.86M alloc ops/s) match none of these figures, and the repo's own docs/tokio-comparison.md reports Zokio at 0.84x Tokio on task scheduling and 0.59x on I/O, so the published ratios are invalid.
status_note: Stale since 2025-07-22 (170 commits, 5 stars, no issues filed). It is MIT-licensed but pinned to Zig 0.14 and ships without a working libxev submodule setup, so vendoring it means fixing the build yourself.
